summary: Gives requirements for Diameter overload control. Existing mechanisms do not handle overload well, so servers can get progressively worse; the document describes the limits and lists requirements for new mechanisms.

eli5.summary: When a shop is too busy, it should be able to say please come back later instead of sinking.

questions: what to do when a diameter server is overloaded
what does diameter too busy mean
subtitle: Why Diameter's built-in busy signals fall short, and the 34 requirements a proper overload control mechanism must meet.

tldr.problem: A Diameter node that has too little capacity to handle its requests can only go silent or answer DIAMETER_TOO_BUSY, so clients cannot be told to slow down gradually and the overload can get worse.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the causes and effects of overload, deployment scenarios, mobile network case studies and the shortcomings of the existing mechanisms, then lists 34 numbered requirements (REQ 1 to REQ 34) for a new overload indication mechanism.
tldr.outcome: It specifies requirements only, not a solution. The requirement keywords describe what future specifications must do, not interoperability of implementations.

today: RFC 7068 is an Informational document and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements for a future overload control mechanism and does not define that mechanism itself.

sections.title: What Overload Means for Diameter
sections.content:
A Diameter node (RFC 6733) is overloaded when it lacks the resources to process all the requests it receives. It then needs to gracefully reduce its load, typically by advising clients to reduce traffic for a time; otherwise it keeps spending resources parsing and answering messages and the overload gets progressively worse. The memo draws on SIP overload control work (RFC 5390, RFC 6357), SS7 experience and 3GPP studies.

The listed causes include inadequate capacity, dependency failures (such as a failed DNS server or database), component failures in a cluster, network-initiated and subscriber-initiated traffic floods, and denial-of-service attacks. When a node fails, many messages can be lost during failover, and retries can fill local queues, so nodes need to shed load before critical failure.

The memo is about application-layer overload, which is distinct from network congestion. Congestion is left to TCP and SCTP, and signaling overload on non-Diameter protocols is out of scope.
sections.eli5: When too many people line up at a counter, the clerk needs a way to tell the line to slow down before everything jams up.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The scenarios assume a client sends requests to a server, and that a cluster acts as a single node. They are deliberately simplified.

  • Peer-to-peer: one client and one server, where the client must queue or itself become overloaded; several servers, where an overloaded one should be able to ask the client to divert only part of its traffic; and several realm and application combinations, where a server may be overloaded for Application A but not B, yet also needs a way to say it is overloaded for all applications.
  • Agent: a relay or proxy sits between client and servers. The agent should usually handle upstream overload transparently and not pass it on in a way that makes the client think the agent itself is overloaded, but when a request names a specific server through Destination-Host, the client may need to be told that server is overloaded.
  • Interconnect: operators connected through a service such as IPX may not want to share topology or operational details, and the interconnect elements may not support overload control, so information may need to pass through without being acted on.
sections.eli5: The paper draws different shops: one with one clerk, one with several, and one with a manager in the middle. Each needs its own way of saying it is too busy.

sections.title: Case Studies and Existing Mechanisms
sections.content:
In mobile networks, high signaling load has caused overload at Diameter-based HLRs and HSSs. The memo says aggressive smartphone registration logic generates ten times the HSS signaling load of a non-smartphone. A 3GPP study (TR 23.843) describes traffic storms when devices switch between radio technologies, floods after a core element fails or recovers, and floods caused by events or catastrophes.

Diameter's existing signs of trouble are implicit, meaning a missing response (helped by the watchdog of RFC 3539), and explicit: the DIAMETER_TOO_BUSY and DIAMETER_UNABLE_TO_DELIVER errors, and a Disconnect-Peer-Request with Disconnect-Cause of BUSY. Congestion-managed transport is not the right level to handle server overload.
sections.eli5: Right now a busy shop can only stay silent or say busy. Both are too blunt, and the paper explains exactly why.

sections.title: Problems With the Current Mechanisms
sections.content:
None of the existing mechanisms lets a node shed load as it approaches overload; at best it can say it must stop receiving requests, as if it had failed.

  • The implicit mechanism tells the client only when it is effectively too late, and cannot tell node overload from network congestion.
  • DIAMETER_TOO_BUSY is ambiguous about what a client should do next. RFC 6733 says to try another peer but does not say future messages should be affected, and it gives no guidance on how long to wait before retrying. It can only signal overload for the whole server, not for one application, and it has no durational validity.
  • Agents handle the error as a protocol error, and a downstream peer may stop sending all requests to the agent even though the agent can still reach other servers.
  • DIAMETER_UNABLE_TO_DELIVER and DPR with BUSY also lack scope, cause and duration.

The memo also says a solution should be extensible and application independent, since a single overload algorithm may not suit every scenario.
sections.eli5: A sign that just says busy does not say for how long, or which counter. So people either keep queueing or leave entirely.

sections.title: The Solution Requirements
sections.content:
The 34 requirements are grouped into general, performance, heterogeneous support, granular control, priority and policy, security, and flexibility. A few examples:

  • General: a way to exchange load and overload information regardless of application (REQ 1, REQ 2), independently in each direction (REQ 4), and with minimal new configuration (REQ 6).
  • Performance: stability and convergence without oscillation after overload ends (REQ 7), telling current from stale information (REQ 8), and no substantial extra work for an overloaded node (REQ 13).
  • Incremental deployment: it must work in a mixed environment, and not leave things materially worse than without it (REQ 16, REQ 17).
  • Granular control: graded throttling because overload is not binary (REQ 22), and load levels even when not overloaded (REQ 24).
  • Flexibility: overload expressible at least per Diameter node, realm and Diameter application (REQ 31), extensibility (REQ 32), and a mandatory default algorithm (REQ 33).

Priority requirements say the base specification should give general guidance, such as favoring existing sessions over new ones, with details left to applications (REQ 25), and local policy must not be prevented (REQ 26).
sections.eli5: The rules say the busy sign must work for every kind of customer, say how busy you are, say when it is over, and not make the clerk even busier.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Load and overload information directly changes node behavior and may be commercially sensitive, so it needs protection. The memo notes that the Diameter base specification lacks end-to-end security, which makes it hard for non-adjacent nodes to check who owns load information.

  • Access control: senders should authenticate and authorize receivers (REQ 28, REQ 29).
  • Denial of service: falsely reported overload could cause a large disruption with few messages (REQ 27, REQ 30).
  • Replay and man-in-the-middle: messages could be replayed at the wrong time or to other nodes; TLS and/or IPsec may be desirable.
  • Compromised hosts: impact on other nodes should be minimized.
sections.eli5: A fake busy sign could shut down a perfectly good shop, so the real sign has to be something only the shop can put up, and not just anyone may read it.

items.title: General
items.text: Exchange load and overload information, independent of application.

items.title: Performance
items.text: Stability, stale-versus-current information and rapid feedback.

items.title: Priority and policy
items.text: Guidance on message priority; local policy not prevented.

items.title: Security
items.text: No new vulnerabilities; no assumption that all nodes are trusted.

items.title: Flexibility
items.text: Node, realm and application granularity, extensibility, a default algorithm.
